name: Rangitoto Summit Track
description:
The walk up Auckland's youngest volcano starts at Rangitoto Wharf and climbs steadily across old lava fields and pōhutukawa forest to the summit crater, with views over the Hauraki Gulf and the city. DOC lists it as 7km return with a 250m climb on rough, loose ground, and most people take about an hour each way. There are toilets at the wharf and near the summit.

Fullers360 ferries leave the Downtown Ferry Terminal (Piers 13 and 14) at 9.30am, 10.30am and 12.15pm on weekdays and 9.15am, 10.30am and 12.15pm at weekends and on public holidays, with some sailings via Devonport. The crossing takes about 25 minutes. Adult returns are $63, children 5 to 15 $28.50 and a family of two adults and two children $149. You must book ahead, as same-day walk-on tickets aren't sold, everyone has a biosecurity check before boarding, and there are no shops, drinking water or rubbish bins on the island.
Local tip: The last ferry back leaves at 3.30pm on weekdays and 4pm at weekends, and there's no other way off, so note the time before you set off. Take plenty of water and a hat, as there's little shade on the lava.
hoursNote: Ferries daily except Christmas Day; last return about 3.30pm weekdays, 4pm weekends; no water, food or bins on the island

name: Rangitoto Lava Caves
description:
A short side trip off the Rangitoto Summit Track leads to lava tunnels formed as the outside of the volcano's lava flows cooled and hardened while molten rock kept flowing inside. The signposted turnoff is about 45 minutes up from the wharf, and the caves are another 500m, about 15 minutes, so allow about an hour from Rangitoto Wharf.

Inside it's dark, jagged and uneven, with low ceilings, so mind your head, and keep off the loose rocks. DOC says the caves are a good option for kids, as long as you keep them close. Entry is free, and the only cost is the Fullers360 ferry to the island.
Local tip: Bring a proper torch or headlamp, as DOC advises, and wear sturdy shoes rather than sandals. A phone light works, but you'll want your hands free on the rocks.
hoursNote: Open whenever the island is accessible by ferry; 15 min one way off the Summit Track; bring a torch

name: Home Bay Campsite, Motutapu Island
description:
A large, grassy DOC campsite at Home Bay on Motutapu, the island joined to Rangitoto by a causeway. There are no marked sites, so you book for your party and pick a spot, with room for up to 262 people. Facilities are basic, with non-flush toilets and tap water that DOC says to boil for at least three minutes, and there are no showers, power or bins. Fires are banned, but gas cookers are fine.

It costs $10 a night for adults and $5 for children 5 to 17, and you must book online, with no spaces kept for walk-ups (same-day online bookings close at 8pm). Public ferries to Islington Bay are limited, so most campers take the Fullers360 ferry to Rangitoto Wharf and walk in, about 3 hours on the Motutapu Walkway, or 1.5 hours from Islington Bay Wharf. The vehicle road from the south is closed after storm damage, so stick to the coastal walkway.
Local tip: Pack everything in and out, rubbish included, and check your gear for seeds and soil before you leave the mainland, as Motutapu is pest-free. Takahē are often spotted around Home Bay.
hoursNote: Book online before arriving; $10 adult, $5 child per night; non-flush toilets; boil water; no fires; about 3 hr walk from Rangitoto Wharf

name: Tiritiri Matangi Island
description:
An open island sanctuary in the Hauraki Gulf, covered in replanted bush and kept free of pests, where rare native birds live in the open and often come close to the tracks. Takahē, kōkako, hihi and tīeke (saddleback) are all here. Tracks from the visitor centre, next to New Zealand's oldest working lighthouse, first lit in 1865, take from 10 minutes to 2 hours.

The Explore ferry leaves Viaduct Harbour Wednesday to Sunday and on public holidays, calling at Gulf Harbour, and takes about 80 minutes. Adults pay $110, children 5 to 15 $55 and a family $275. You get about 4 hours 20 minutes on the island on weekdays (9am departure, back at 4pm) and just over 6 hours at weekends (8.30am departure, back at 5.20pm). Volunteer guided walks cost $15 for adults and $5 for children when booked with your ferry ticket.
Local tip: Book well ahead from November to April. No food is sold on the island, so bring lunch in sealed containers and scrub your shoes for the biosecurity check. There's free tea and coffee at the visitor centre, but no rubbish bins.
hoursNote: Ferry Wed to Sun and public holidays, year round; departs Viaduct Harbour 9am weekdays, 8.30am weekends; no food sold on the island; no pets or bikes

name: Onetangi Beach
description:
Waiheke's longest beach: about 2km of golden sand on the north coast, with clear water, usually gentle waves and safe swimming. Even on a busy summer weekend there's plenty of room to spread out.

The beach reserve has toilets, changing rooms, picnic tables and barbecues, and there are café-bars on The Strand for lunch or a drink, with roadside parking. AT buses 50A and 50B run from Matiatia wharf through Oneroa, Surfdale and Ostend to Onetangi.
Local tip: Climb the Jacob's Ladder steps from the beach for a view back along the bay, then cool off with a swim.
hoursNote: Open any time; buses 50A and 50B from Matiatia; roadside parking

name: Oneroa Beach
description:
The main beach below Oneroa village, Waiheke's small town centre, and the closest swimming beach to the Matiatia ferry wharf, about 15 minutes' walk away. A curve of sand faces north across Oneroa Bay, with toilets and outdoor showers at both ends.

Next door, Little Oneroa has a playground, toilets, a gas barbecue and a sheltered patch of sand, with a fish and chip shop and a store across the road. Fullers360 ferries take 40 to 45 minutes from Auckland's Downtown Ferry Terminal to Matiatia, and buses 50A, 50B, 501 and 502 run from the wharf into the village.
Local tip: Stop at Island Gelato at 106b Ocean View Road in the village, open from 11am on weekdays and 10am at weekends, but closed on Wednesdays.
hoursNote: Open any time; buses 50A and 50B from Matiatia; toilets, showers and playground at Little Oneroa

name: Matiatia to Oneroa Headland Walk
description:
A coastal section of Te Ara Hura, Waiheke's round-the-island trail, that starts beside the ferry terminal. It climbs over the headland past Mokemoke Pā, a defensive site used from the 1500s to the 1700s, then drops to Cable Bay and Owhanake Bay before finishing at Oneroa Bay, with views across the Gulf to Rangitoto, Motutapu and Rakino.

It's about 5km and takes 1.5 to 2 hours on grass and dirt paths, with a long climb of steps from Cable Bay and some steep drops close to the cliff edge, so wear proper shoes and watch small children. From the terminal, turn left towards the dinghy racks and follow the signs. A free audio guide for the walk is on the STQRY app.
Local tip: The start at Matiatia is cut off for about 1.5 hours either side of high tide, so check the tide times before you get off the ferry, then finish with lunch in Oneroa.
hoursNote: Free, any time except about 1.5 hr either side of high tide at Matiatia; about 5 km one way; steep sections

name: Dragonfired, Little Oneroa
description:
A wood-fired pizza and pocketbread kitchen beside the playground and beach at Little Oneroa Reserve, and a favourite cheap feed on an island better known for long winery lunches. Take your food onto the grass or the sand.

A margherita is $18, with venison pepperoni, garlic salami or ham for $6 extra and other toppings for $4, and a gluten-free base is $2 more. Calzone, pocketbreads and polenta boxes run from $19 to $23, and garlic pizza bread is $8. It's open daily in summer and Friday to Sunday from 11am to 7pm in winter, weather permitting.
Local tip: Text your order ahead on 021 922 289 to skip the wait, and guard your pizza closely, as the gulls here are bold.
hoursNote: Summer 7 days 12pm to 8pm; winter Fri to Sun 11am to 7pm, weather permitting

name: Palm Beach
description:
A sheltered, family-friendly bay on the north coast between Oneroa and Onetangi, with about 600m of soft sand, clear water, usually small waves and safe swimming. Palm Beach Reserve on Palm Road has toilets, a playground, picnic tables and a gas barbecue.

Bus 502 runs from Matiatia through Oneroa to Palm Beach. Little Palm, at the western end beyond the rocks, is a well-known clothing-optional beach.
Local tip: Parking is limited on fine days, so come by bus or bike if you can, and bring something for the barbecue.
hoursNote: Open any time; bus 502 from Matiatia; toilets, outdoor showers and drinking water at Palm Beach Reserve; limited parking

name: Mudbrick Vineyard Cellar Door
description:
One of Waiheke's best-known vineyards, at 126 Church Bay Road a short ride from Matiatia wharf, with gardens and wide views. You don't need a restaurant booking to enjoy it, as the cellar door takes walk-ins for tastings, every day from 10am to 5pm, for groups of six or fewer.

Tastings take 20 to 40 minutes and cost $31 for the Mudbrick or Icon tastings, $23 for the South Island tasting and $22 for sweet wines, with a surcharge on public holidays. Groups of seven or more should call or email ahead. Private vineyard tours cost $50 a person (minimum six) and take 45 minutes, and the Archive bistro is the more relaxed option if you want to eat.
Local tip: In fine weather, ask to taste in Robyn's Glasshouse and garden, and come early on summer weekends.
hoursNote: Tastings 7 days 10am to 5pm; no booking needed for groups under 7; public holiday surcharge

name: Man O' War Vineyards
description:
A beachfront tasting room and restaurant at Man O' War Bay, on the quiet eastern end of Waiheke, about 40 to 45 minutes' drive from Matiatia. Wine tastings and long lunches with sea views are the draw, and it's a good place to break a day exploring the less-visited east of the island.

It pairs well with a walk at nearby Stony Batter. Explore also runs a direct ferry from Viaduct Harbour to Man O' War Bay, about 90 minutes each way, Wednesday to Sunday, for $110 for adults and $55 for children, but tastings and meals are booked separately with Man O' War. Opening days vary with the season, so check before you go.
Local tip: Book ahead if you want lunch, especially as a group, as the restaurant fills on fine summer days.
hoursNote: Open daily in summer (from 1 Dec); fewer days in the cooler months, so check first; about 45 min drive from Matiatia

name: Stony Batter Historic Reserve
description:
A WWII coastal battery on farmland at the eastern end of Waiheke, with old gun emplacements among huge boulders, a nīkau palm grove and 360 degree views east over the islands towards the Coromandel. From the car park off Man O' War Bay Road it's a 10 to 25 minute walk across farmland to the tunnel complex, and a separate advanced track drops to the gravel beach at Opopo Bay (1 hour 40 minutes return, with parts overgrown after storm damage).

The underground tunnels closed to tours on 19 April 2026, and in May 2026 DOC granted a 10-year concession to a joint venture of Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki and Man O' War Vineyards. The reserve and tracks stay open, and you can join a waitlist on the Stony Batter Tunnels website for when tours return. It's about 40 minutes' drive from Matiatia, and there's no public transport this far east.
Local tip: Combine it with a tasting or lunch at Man O' War nearby, and bring water and sturdy shoes.
hoursNote: Reserve and tracks open; tunnel tours paused since April 2026 pending new operators; 10 to 25 min walk from the car park

name: eRide Waiheke E-Bike Hire
description:
E-bike hire inside the Matiatia ferry terminal, opposite the Fullers ticket office, so you can step off the boat and ride. Waiheke is hilly, and an e-bike makes the climbs between beaches and vineyards manageable. Each hire includes a helmet, a bike fitting, a safety briefing, route suggestions and access to a guide app, and the bikes have a range of 50 to 80km.

Hire starts from $119 for the 5 Bays ride and $140 for the full-day Man O' War ride, with multi-day hire from $198. Fullers360 ferries take 40 to 45 minutes from Auckland's Downtown Ferry Terminal, and a standard adult return is $65, or $48.50 off-peak if you leave Auckland from 1pm or Waiheke from 7pm. If you'd rather not ride, AT buses meet the ferries: the 50A and 50B go to Oneroa, Ostend and Onetangi, the 502 to Palm Beach, and you can tap on with a contactless card or phone.
Local tip: Book online to get away faster, and save some battery for the hills on the way back to the ferry.
hoursNote: Daily 9am to 5.30pm at Matiatia ferry terminal; book online

name: Poukaraka Flats Campground, Whakanewha
description:
A large, flat and sheltered council campground behind the beach in Whakanewha Regional Park, at 75 Gordons Road on Waiheke's south coast, with bush walks up to the Cascades. It's vehicle-based, with room for up to 80 people, a flush toilet, cold showers, drinking water and a free gas barbecue, but no power and no bins.

Sites are $18 a night for adults and $7 for children, infants are free, and the maximum stay is seven nights. Bookings open six months ahead and summer dates fill fast. The campground is behind a locked gate, with the code in your booking confirmation, and the park gates open from 6am to 9pm in daylight saving (7pm otherwise). Waiheke has no designated freedom camping sites or public dump station, and camping isn't allowed in reserves or regional parks, so this is the island's best budget option.
Local tip: Swim around high tide, which the council says is the best time at these beaches.
hoursNote: Book ahead; $18 adult, $7 child per night; max 7 nights; check in 11am; flush toilets, cold showers, drinking water; no bins

name: Waiheke Backpackers Hostel
description:
A relaxed hostel at 421 Sea View Road in Onetangi, owned and run by Auckland Council and a short walk from the beach. Recent guests rate it highly, scoring it 9.3 on Hostelworld, with top marks for cleanliness and friendly staff.

It has four-bed and two-bed mixed dorms, doubles (one with an ensuite) and a family room, a fully equipped kitchen, free wifi, laundry ($4 wash, $4 dry), a TV lounge, free parking and a garden with hammocks and bean bags. The council lists bunks from $33 and doubles from $85 a night. Check-in is from 2pm to 6pm and check-out by 10.30am.
Local tip: The hostel rents out e-bikes too, which saves sorting out hire at the wharf, and it's a short walk down to Onetangi Beach for sunset.
hoursNote: Book online; reception 09 372 7003; shared bathrooms; free parking

name: Kaitoke Hot Springs Track
description:
Free natural hot springs in the bush on Aotea Great Barrier Island, reached by an easy, flat walk from Whangaparapara Road across the Kaitoke wetlands. DOC rates the track easiest and allows about an hour one way, and it ends at pools dammed where two branches of Kaitoke Creek meet, with a toilet just before the springs.

The pools are shallow and the temperature varies, with hotter rock pools further upstream, and the water can be very hot in places. DOC advises you not to put your head under. Getting to the Barrier is a trip in itself: SeaLink ferries take about 4.5 hours from Auckland to Tryphena, sailing up to seven times a week in summer and four in the cooler months, or Barrier Air flies to Claris in about 30 minutes.
Local tip: Bring plenty of drinking water, and keep your face out of the pools.
hoursNote: Free, open any time; about 1 hr one way from Whangaparapara Road; do not put your head under the water

name: Windy Canyon
description:
A short walk on Aotea Great Barrier Island through a rocky canyon to lookouts over the Okiwi Basin and Whangapoua Beach and estuary, with views east towards Kaitoke and Medlands beaches. It starts at the top of Whangapoua Hill on Aotea Road and takes about 15 minutes one way to the canyon.

Keen walkers can carry on along Palmer's Track to the summit of Hirakimata (Mt Hobson), about 3 hours return. Beyond the canyon it becomes a tramping track with steep sections that DOC warns carry a real fall risk, including a slippery rock lookout, and there's no water on the track.
Local tip: If you're heading past the canyon, swap sneakers for proper boots, as DOC advises, and carry 1 to 2 litres of water each.
hoursNote: Free, open any time; 15 min one way to the canyon; Palmer's Track to Hirakimata 3 hr return; no water

name: Medlands Beach Campsite
description:
A DOC campsite set back from Medlands Beach on the east coast of Aotea Great Barrier Island, surrounded by farmland, holiday homes and dunes and overlooking a tidal stream. There are no marked sites, so you book for your party and find a spot, with room for up to 120 people.

Adults pay $18 a night and children 5 to 17 $9, infants are free, and you must book online before you arrive, as no spaces are kept for walk-ups. Facilities are simple: non-flush toilets, cold showers, a covered cooking shelter and untreated tap water you should boil, so bring your own cooker. Dogs aren't allowed. A camp host is on site from Christmas to mid-February, and there are shops and cafés about 4km north and 6km south, along narrow gravel roads.
Local tip: It's pack in, pack out, food scraps included. Buy the orange council rubbish bags at a local shop, then drop them at the Claris landfill for free.
hoursNote: Book online; $18 adult, $9 child per night; non-flush toilets, cold showers; boil water; no dogs; pack out rubbish
